children: is warning that America's AI infrastructure boom could become a new inflation problem for the Federal Reserve, even as he pushes back against the idea that data centers are responsible for the economy's current resilience. His comments sharpen a critical question for investors: whether unprecedented AI capital spending boosts productivity fast enough to justify easier monetary policy, or instead keeps rates higher by overheating parts of the economy.

Goolsbee said employment conditions remain relatively stable, but credited consumers rather than AI investment. I think that's been largely not the result of AI data centers, for much ballyhoo it's the U.S. consumer. Broad-based consumer spending growth is the thing that has kept the economy solid and stable.
The risk is what happens as the data-center buildout expands.

Goolsbee described the sector as very hot, arguing that enormous AI investments are already competing with other businesses for scarce construction workers, HVAC equipment and other resources. Companies across the Chicago Fed's district have told him they are scaling back projects because those inputs have become too expensive or difficult to obtain.
That matters because AI could have two very different effects on interest rates.

If the productivity lands on us in an unexpected way, inflation goes down, and rates can go down, Goolsbee said. But if expectations and investment surge before those productivity gains materialize, he warned the result could instead be old-fashioned overheating in the short run.

. August payrolls are due September 4, followed by producer prices September 10 and CPI September 11.

services inflation, wages and construction costs

higher. Softer inflation would support Goolsbee's productivity-friendly scenario and lower-rate expectations. Persistent price pressure, however, could strengthen the case for keeping policy restrictive and turn the AI spending boom into an unexpected headwind for valuations.

title: Fed's Goolsbee Flags Dangerous Side of AI Spending
